drafts.subject: chr:entity:marcus-vipsanius-agrippa
drafts.quotation: Octavian's maritime fleet, led by Marcus Agrippa
drafts.rationale: The article says Octavian's fleet was led by Marcus Agrippa. 'Marcus Agrippa' is an alias of Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa, and 'led' means he directed the fleet in the action, so I drafted commanded rather than formal authority.
drafts.relevance: Through the military lens, it names who commanded Octavian's fleet at Actium.

drafts.subject: chr:entity:augustus
drafts.quotation: the climax of over a decade of rivalry between Octavian and Mark Antony
drafts.rationale: The article calls the battle the climax of a rivalry between Octavian and Mark Antony. The article uses 'Octavian' for the future emperor, so I mapped it to the Augustus person entity. The time is the article's vague phrase and is not converted to a date.
drafts.relevance: Through the military lens, it frames the battle as the culmination of the long rivalry between the two commanders.

drafts.subject: chr:entity:mark-antony
drafts.quotation: Mark Antony possessed 500 ships and 70,000 infantry
drafts.rationale: The article says Antony possessed 500 ships in early 31 BC, which shows formal authority over his fleet but not who directed it in action. The figure of 500 ships is this article's own voice and is not reconciled with other figures.
drafts.relevance: Shows who held supreme authority over the fleet that fought at Actium, and its stated size, through the military lens.
ambiguities: The article describes the fleet Antony possessed in early 31 BC, before the battle; the entity is the fleet as it fought at Actium.

drafts.subject: chr:entity:antony-fleet-at-actium
drafts.quotation: Antony's fleet sailed out through the straits of Actium in a desperate attempt to break free of the naval blockade, but faced, fought and was eventually routed by Octavian's fleet of smaller, more maneuverable ships.
drafts.rationale: The article says Antony's fleet sailed out, then faced, fought and was routed by Octavian's fleet. The two fleets are therefore enemies in the naval action. The passage gives no year for this action, so the claim is undated.
drafts.relevance: Through the military lens, it names the two opposing fleets in the naval action of the battle.

notes.note: The article explains the outcome by the smaller, more maneuverable ships of Octavian's fleet and presents Antony's sortie as a desperate attempt to break the blockade.
notes.quotation: routed by Octavian's fleet of smaller, more maneuverable ships

notes.note: The article gives the political reading of the break between Octavian and Antony that led to the war: Octavian and most of the Senate saw Antony as heading a separatist movement. It names no force or command, so no claim is drafted.
notes.quotation: Octavian and the majority of the Roman Senate saw Antony as leading a separatist movement that threatened to break the Roman Republic's unity.

drafts.subject: chr:entity:mark-antony
drafts.quotation: Antony had been the most important and most successful senior officer in Caesar's army (magister equitum)
drafts.rationale: The passage says Antony was Caesar's most important and most successful senior officer. In this article 'Caesar' used alone is Julius Caesar, and 'Antony' is Mark Antony. The office magister equitum is named but no time is stated, so the claim is drafted without a role or time.
drafts.relevance: Shows Antony's earlier place in Caesar's army, which the passage ties to his hold on Caesar's soldiers and veterans, a source of the military backing he brought to the Actium confrontation.

notes.note: The article reports that Plutarch and Dio describe desertion and disease in Antony's camp. This is the article's account of those two authors, and it bears on the manpower of Antony's forces.

notes.note: The article describes the composition of Antony's fleet as mainly quinqueremes with some quadriremes. It calls them heavier and wider than Octavian's ships, so better gun platforms but less manoeuvrable.
notes.quotation: his ships were mainly the standard Roman warship, quinqueremes with smaller quadriremes, heavier and wider than Octavian's, making them ideal weapon platforms.

notes.note: Gives the article's account of the composition and armament of Antony's heavy galleys: a "ten" flagship and a heavily manned "eight" with marines, archers and ballistae. It is a general description of the fleet, not an action.
notes.quotation: Antony's personal flagship, like his admirals', was a "ten".

notes.note: Says Agrippa's harpax, a grappling and boarding device, helped Octavian's side deal with Antony's hard-to-board galleys.
notes.quotation: The harpax, Agrippa's device made for grappling and boarding enemy ships, made this task a bit easier.

notes.note: The article reads the tactical balance as follows: Antony's ships were hard to ram or board, so the only way to disable one was to smash its oars. Their lack of manoeuvrability was their weakness, because an isolated ship could be swamped by boarders.
notes.quotation: Antony's ships' main weakness was their lack of manoeuvrability; such a ship, once isolated from its fleet, could be swamped with boarding attacks.

notes.note: Records manpower: many of Antony's ships had too few rowers because of a malaria outbreak while waiting for Octavian's fleet.
notes.quotation: Also, many of his ships were undermanned with rowing crews; there had been a severe malaria outbreak while they were waiting for Octavian's fleet to arrive.

notes.note: The article gives the composition of Octavian's fleet: mostly smaller Liburnian vessels. This is the force-composition counterpart to its description of Antony's larger ships.
notes.quotation: Octavian's fleet was largely made up of smaller "Liburnian" vessels.

notes.note: The article states that Octavian's crews were better trained, professional, well-fed and rested, which it uses to explain the fleet's tactical advantage.
